title: Bolt a coupling nut to an upright plate through its hole with an M10 screw, head and nut both snug
instruction: Fasten the screw and the nut together through the hole in the plate, with the screw's head on one side and the nut on the other, until both are snug against the plate, then let go of both.
context: Bolting parts together through a hole is one of the most common assembly steps, in workshops, furniture assembly and maintenance: the nut on the far side has to be kept from turning while the screw is turned in, or the screw does not go in.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed grey steel plate standing upright on the centre line, its faces turned to the left and right arms: 10 cm front to back, 25 cm tall, 8 mm thick, centred 26 cm forward, on a dark foot 10 x 8 cm. A 12 mm square hole (a clearance hole for M10) goes through it, centred 26 cm forward and 20 cm above the table, with a yellow square printed round it on both faces. (2) A loose zinc-plated steel M10 x 20 hex-head screw (ISO 4017, M10 x 1.5 thread), 25 g: the head 16 mm across flats and 6.4 mm tall, the shank 10 mm across and 20 mm long, its last 3 mm chamfered narrower (8 mm). It stands head up, its shank in the 11 mm square bore of a fixed dark block 3 x 3 cm and 2.5 cm tall, centred 24 cm forward and 12 cm right of the centre line. (3) A loose zinc-plated steel M10 coupling nut (DIN 6334, M10 x 1.5 thread), 40 g: 17 mm across flats and 30 mm long, its thread countersunk to 15 mm over its last 3 mm at each end. It stands on end on a fixed dark block 3 x 3 cm and 2.5 cm tall, centred 24 cm forward and 12 cm left of the centre line, round a short peg (5 mm across, 3 mm tall). The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The screw's turn against the nut, about the screw's axis, is followed after every control step. The thread catches when, with the screw's tip at least 1 mm into the nut's bore and the two lined up (axes within 10 degrees and 4 mm), the screw turns a quarter turn clockwise as seen from its head; turns are counted from then on, net, clockwise counting positive. Through: the screw's axis crosses the plate within 4 mm of the hole's centre, with its head on one side and its tip past the other face. Snug: the head and the nut together stand no more than 2 mm off the plate's faces. A gripper has let go when its fingertip centre (TCP) is at least 4 cm from both the screw's head and the nut. 1.0: through, caught in the nut on the far side, turned at least 1.5 turns, snug, and both grippers let go; 0.5: through and caught in the nut on the far side, turned at least half a turn; 0.25: through; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the screw and the nut still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed: unscrew the screw, stand it head up in its holder and stand the nut back on its peg.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The thread is not geometry: the shank is a plain 10 mm cylinder in the nut's plain 11 mm hexagonal bore, and a joint switched on once the thread catches keeps the nut on the screw's axis, adds thread friction (0.15 N m s/rad) and draws the nut 5 mm per turn (3.3 times M10's 1.5 mm pitch, to keep a trial short; spring 2,000 N/m, at most 20 N). Plate, holder and stand are fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
